title: A hymn in Majh
hook: Majh holds Guru Arjan's letters and the Barah Maha

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Majh, and your line was punjabi longing. Did you send that plain message to someone you miss? Today, the longing gets words. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

A moment, and a year. One is a single moment of missing someone; the other is a whole year, coming back around. Raga Majh holds a hymn of each, and Guru Arjan wrote both. One is a set of letters from a son far from his father. The other walks through the twelve months, one by one. Year two read each on its own. Today, side by side, in the raga they share. Today: a hymn in Majh.
screen: `A MOMENT, AND A YEAR.` → `TWO HYMNS OF GURU ARJAN.` → `ONE RAGA: MAJH.`

segments.voice: First, the letters. Tradition says young Arjan was sent to Lahore by his father, Guru Ram Das, and told to stay until he was called. The call didn't come, and he wrote home in verse. In the Granth the verses stand as one shabad in Majh. My mind longs for a sight of the Guru, the first stanza says in effect; it cries like the rainbird for rain. And in the third, the longing is measured in a single moment: when I can't meet you for even a moment, it's a dark age for me. A moment, stretched into an age. Then the Barah Maha, the song of the twelve months, also in Majh, also Guru Arjan's. Its months begin with Chet: in Chet, it says in paraphrase, remember the Lord of the world, and a deep joy comes. Month follows month, and each one asks the same thing of the soul, the bride waiting for her Lord: is this the month we meet? Here the longing is measured in months, the whole turning year. Hear the two together and Majh starts to make sense. One hymn counts moments. The other counts months. Both are about distance from the beloved, and both end by finding him near. The letters close with the Lord found in the singer's own home. The months close by saying that months, days and moments are blessed for the one the Lord looks on with grace. The raga's homesick sound fits both. That's today's line: letters of longing. Tomorrow, a raga whose section runs on for page after page.
screen: `THE LETTERS: A MOMENT IS AN AGE.` · `THE BARAH MAHA: MONTH AFTER MONTH.` · `MOMENTS AND MONTHS, ONE LONGING.` · then, large: `LETTERS OF LONGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Majh shabad. If you can, find a recording of Guru Arjan's letters, the shabad that begins with the mind longing for the Guru's sight, or of the Barah Maha in Majh, and let it play through the sit. Don't track every word. Listen for where the voice reaches, and where it rests. If there's no recording near you, try the two scales of longing in your own life. First a moment: one person you'd like to see today. Then a year: one thing you've been waiting for since last spring. Hold each for a few breaths, without fixing anything. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the word that answers both. The bell holds the time.
screen: `A MOMENT: WHO TODAY?` → `A YEAR: WHAT SINCE LAST SPRING?`

segments.voice: A hymn in Majh. Guru Arjan's letters, where a moment apart is an age, and his Barah Maha, where the months pass in waiting, two shapes of longing in one raga. Today's word.
Your line: letters of longing. Today, write three lines to someone you miss, a moment's worth, and keep them, even if you never send them. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Guru Arjan's shabad of the letters is sung in kirtan in Raag Majh, and the Barah Maha in Majh is read in some gurdwaras at the start of each month of the Indian calendar, on Sangrand.

fork.setup: you're setting two hymns of longing, one measured in moments, one in months. which raga do you give them?
options: two different ragas, to keep them apart.
the same raga, Majh, with its sound of missing.
no raga, so the words stand alone.
fork.reveal: both stand in Majh, so the same homesick sound carries the son's letters and the soul's year of waiting.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the twelve months, Guru Arjan's song of the year in Raag Majh.

trapdoor: what you thought: Majh holds a story about some letters.
what it means: two hymns of Guru Arjan in one raga, longing measured in moments and in months.

what a scholar hears: the letters (Majh M5, Ang 96–97) and the Barah Maha (Majh M5, from Ang 133) share a raga and a theme, separation and union; the Lahore letter narrative comes from Sikh tradition rather than the text itself.

sources.ref: Majh M5, Ang 96–97 (meraa man lochai gur darsan taaee)
Barah Maha Majh M5, Ang 133 (chet govind araadheeai hovai anand ghanaa)

notes: Day 651 (y2) taught the letters whole and Block I of year two (days 564–578) taught the Barah Maha; this day only sets them side by side as hymns in Majh. Paraphrases follow day 651 for the letters.
Confirm the Barah Maha in Majh (Guru Arjan) begins on Ang 133 with Chet and the paraphrase of its opening line.
'Twelve months' is the composition's own subject (Barah Maha); confirm acceptable under the claims rule.
'Both end by finding him near': the letters' last stanza (found within my own home) and the Barah Maha's close (the month and day are blessed when the meeting comes); confirm the second paraphrase.
howItsDone: Barah Maha read on Sangrand in some gurdwaras; confirm.
Original ਬਾਰਹ ਮਾਹਾ: confirm spelling as in the heading (ਬਾਰਹ ਮਾਹਾ ਮਾਂਝ).

Editor: the Barah Maha has an opening stanza before Chet, so 'it opens with Chet' became 'its months begin with Chet' (teach and myth); the letters' close is in the text, so 'tradition says' dropped there; Barah Maha close re-paraphrased (months, days, moments blessed for the one shown grace); varied the repeated 'earlier on the path' hook line.
